claims.source: Since then, 'Ligulalepis' has been recovered as a stem osteichthyan in most analyses (Davis et al., 2012; Giles et al., 2015b; Giles et al., 2015c; Giles et al., 2017; Long et al., 2015; Lu et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to phylogenetic analyses.

claims.claim: Tip dated analyses employed by King et al., 2017 place 'Ligulalepis' within Actinopterygii with quite strong support.
claims.source: However, tip dated analyses employed by King et al., 2017 place 'Ligulalepis' within Actinopterygii with quite strong support.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to King et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Scans of AM-F101607 reveal for the first time some of the sutures between the skull roofing bones showing a pattern different in important respects to the previous interpretation.
claims.source: Scans of AM-F101607 reveal for the first time some of the sutures between the skull roofing bones (Figure 1) showing a pattern different in important respects to the previous interpretation (Basden and Young, 2001).
claims.evidence: This is based on new CT scan data of the specimen.

claims.claim: No midline suture is evident between the postparietals in AM-F101607.
claims.source: No midline suture is evident between the postparietals, but a very faint suture between the parietals is suggested.
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the CT scan data.

claims.claim: A very faint suture between the parietals is suggested in AM-F101607.
claims.source: No midline suture is evident between the postparietals, but a very faint suture between the parietals is suggested.
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the CT scan data.

claims.claim: The presence of middle and posterior pitlines, and the supraorbital canals extending to the posterior edge of the postparietals, is confirmed in ANU V3628.
claims.source: The presence of middle and posterior pitlines, and the supraorbital canals extending to the posterior edge of the postparietals, is confirmed in ANU V3628.
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the CT scan data of ANU V3628.

claims.claim: ANU V3628 preserves the previously unknown anterior portion of the skull roof.
claims.source: ANU V3628 preserves the previously unknown anterior portion of the skull roof (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on direct observation of the specimen.

claims.claim: A pineal foramen is preserved in ANU V3628.
claims.source: A pineal foramen is preserved, but due to a crack in the specimen it is unclear if a separate pineal plate was present.
claims.evidence: This is based on direct observation of the specimen.

claims.claim: The profile of the snout has a sharply downturned anterior face.
claims.source: The profile of the snout has a sharply downturned anterior face (Figure 3), as is general for gnathostomes (Gardiner, 1984; Long, 1988; Zhu et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the specimen and comparison with other gnathostomes.

claims.claim: There is an abrupt change in ornamentation on the snout, from short anteriorly directed ridges to elongate transverse ridges.
claims.source: There is an abrupt change in ornamentation on the snout, from short anteriorly directed ridges to elongate transverse ridges (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is based on direct observation of the specimen.

claims.claim: A similar pattern of ornamentation change is known in Dialipina.
claims.source: A similar pattern is known in Dialipina (Schultze and Cumbaa, 2001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Schultze and Cumbaa, 2001.

claims.claim: The incurrent nostrils are large and widely separated from the excurrent nostrils in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: The incurrent nostrils are large and widely separated from the excurrent nostrils, which appear to lie entirely within the orbits (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the specimens.

claims.claim: The excurrent nostrils appear to lie entirely within the orbits in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: The incurrent nostrils are large and widely separated from the excurrent nostrils, which appear to lie entirely within the orbits (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the specimens.

claims.claim: In 'Ligulalepis' the opening for the posterior nostril in the endocranium lies directly within the orbit.
claims.source: However, in 'Ligulalepis' the opening for the posterior nostril in the endocranium lies directly within the orbit (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the CT scan data.

claims.claim: 'Ligulalepis' lacks an endoskeletal lamina (postnasal wall) separating the nostril and the orbit.
claims.source: 'Ligulalepis' lacks such a lamina, and in this respect more closely resembles some placoderms such as Parabuchanosteus (Young, 1979) and Dicksonosteus (Goujet, 1984).
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the CT scan data and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: The supraorbital canal extends nearly the full preserved length of the cranium in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: The supraorbital canal (soc) extends nearly the full preserved length of the cranium, terminating a little way posterior to the downturned margin of the snout, and appears to be formed from two separate sections (Figures 1C and 3C).
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the CT scan data.

claims.claim: The supraorbital canal appears to be formed from two separate sections in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: The supraorbital canal (soc) extends nearly the full preserved length of the cranium, terminating a little way posterior to the downturned margin of the snout, and appears to be formed from two separate sections (Figures 1C and 3C).
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the CT scan data.

claims.claim: Tubuli connecting the supraorbital canal to the surface are small and few in number in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: Tubuli connecting the supraorbital canal to the surface are small and few in number.
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the CT scan data.

claims.claim: Tubuli connecting the infraorbital and otic canals to the surface are larger in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: Tubuli connecting the infraorbital (ioc) and otic (otc) canals to the surface are larger (Figure 3D, arrows).
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the CT scan data.

claims.claim: The tubuli do not appear to be branched in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: The tubuli do not appear to be branched (although they may have branched in the skin above the bone), in contrast to the highly branched tubuli of some early sarcopterygians (Bjerring, 1972; Clément and Ahlberg, 2010; Jarvik, 1972).
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the CT scan data and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: Anterior to the level of the pineal foramen, the supraorbital sensory canals open to the dorsal surface of the cranium in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: Anterior to the level of the pineal foramen, the supraorbital sensory canals open to the dorsal surface of the cranium (Figure 2), although the canal itself is housed in a ridge on the visceral surface of the skull roof.
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the specimen.

claims.claim: The condition of supraorbital canals opening to the dorsal surface is similar to that in Achoania, Guiyu, and Psarolepis.
claims.source: This is similar to the condition in Achoania (Zhu et al., 2001), Guiyu (Zhu et al., 2009), and Psarolepis (Yu, 1998), and may be equivalent to the 'nasal pitlines' described for Mimipiscis (Gardiner, 1984, fig. 41, 102), although in Mimipiscis the supraorbital canals continue anterior to the pitline.
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison with other taxa cited.

claims.claim: Scans show no evidence for a preopercular canal in either specimen of 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: Basden and Young (2001) described a lateral notch for a preopercular sensory line, however, scans show no evidence for a preopercular canal in either specimen.
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the CT scan data.

claims.claim: A short anterior canal at the intersection of the otic and infraorbital canals is present in ANU V3628.
claims.source: A short anterior canal at the intersection of the otic and infraorbital canals is present in ANU V3628 (Figure 3D: 'P'), but less developed in AM-F101607.
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the CT scan data.

claims.claim: The 'P' canal is present in some acanthodians, for example Acanthodes and some actinopterygians, namely Mimipiscis and Moythomasia.
claims.source: It is present in some acanthodians, for example Acanthodes (Watson, 1937) and some actinopterygians, namely Mimipiscis and Moythomasia (Gardiner, 1984).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: The braincase of 'Ligulalepis' is mostly well ossified, and comprises the basisphenoid, orbitotemporal and otic regions.
claims.source: It is mostly well ossified, and comprises the basisphenoid, orbitotemporal and otic regions.
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the specimens.

claims.claim: The posterior and ventral portion of the braincase, comprising the occiput and basioccipital, is absent in both specimens of 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: The posterior and ventral portion of the braincase, comprising the occiput and basioccipital, is absent in both specimens.
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the specimens.

claims.claim: The orbital region is large, comprising nearly half of total braincase length in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: The orbital region is large, comprising nearly half of total braincase length, and the ethmoid region short.
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the specimens.

claims.claim: The ethmoid region is short in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: The orbital region is large, comprising nearly half of total braincase length, and the ethmoid region short.
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the specimens.

claims.claim: The ethmoid region is separated from the orbitotemporal region by a poorly developed postnasal wall in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: It is separated from the orbitotemporal region by a poorly developed postnasal wall.
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the specimens.

claims.claim: A canal leaves the cranial cavity at the left lateral limit of the pineal opening and extends posterolaterally to open into the orbit in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: A canal leaves the cranial cavity at the left lateral limit of the pineal opening and extends posterolaterally to open into the orbit (Figures 4C–E and 5, acv).
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the CT scan data.

claims.claim: The canal at the left lateral limit of the pineal opening may have housed the anterior cerebral vein in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: This opening was identified by Basden and Young (2001) as for the trochlear nerve (n.IV), but its anterior position suggests it may have housed the anterior cerebral vein.
claims.evidence: This is based on reinterpretation of the anatomy.

claims.claim: The canal for the anterior cerebral vein is present on only the left side in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: This canal is present on only the left side, as in some sarcopterygians such as Latimeria (Robineau, 1975), and various early actinopterygians such as Mimipiscis (Giles and Friedman, 2014) and Kansasiella (Poplin, 1974).
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the specimens and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: The main trunk of the superficial ophthalmic nerve does not enter the orbit in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: However, the main trunk of the superficial ophthalmic nerve does not enter the orbit. It remains within the neurocranium, passing below the supraorbital sensory line (Figures 5 and 6, soph).
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the CT scan data.

claims.claim: The foramina in the orbit of 'Ligulalepis' more likely carried branches of the profundus nerve to the skull roof.
claims.source: Thus, the foramina in the orbit more likely carried branches of the profundus nerve to the skull roof (Figures 3–6, br.prof).
claims.evidence: This is based on reinterpretation of the anatomy.

claims.claim: The internal course of the superficial ophthalmic nerve may be related to the relatively wide interorbital septum in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: The internal course of the superficial ophthalmic nerve may be related to the relatively wide interorbital septum in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis about the relationship between anatomical features.

claims.claim: Below the large opening for the olfactory canal, the posterior face of the nasal capsule is pierced by six foramina in three groups in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: Below the large opening for the olfactory canal, the posterior face of the nasal capsule is pierced by six foramina in three groups.
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the CT scan data.

claims.claim: The two dorsal-most foramina in the nasal capsule most likely transmitted branches of the profundus nerve in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: The two dorsal-most foramina enter the nasal capsule from the orbit, and most likely transmitted branches of the profundus nerve (Figures 4–6, prof).
claims.evidence: This is based on interpretation of the anatomy.

claims.claim: The most ventral three foramina in the nasal capsule may have carried branches of the maxillary and buccal nerves in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: The most ventral three foramina also extends from the orbit, and may have carried branches of the maxillary and buccal nerves (Figures 4–6, br.max).
claims.evidence: This is based on interpretation of the anatomy.

claims.claim: CT scans show that the apparent foramen at the anterior extent of the basisphenoid is in fact blind in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: CT scans show that the apparent foramen at the anterior extent of the basisphenoid (Basden and Young, 2001: fig.7, ?fica) is in fact blind.
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the CT scan data.

claims.claim: The orbitotemporal region is extensive, forming the widest part of the braincase and comprising nearly half the total length in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: The orbitotemporal region is extensive, forming the widest part of the braincase and comprising nearly half the total length.
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the specimens.

claims.claim: A large opening in the orbital wall of AM-F101607 represents the eyestalk attachment area.
claims.source: A large opening in the orbital wall of AM-F101607 represents the eyestalk attachment area, and was recognized as such due to its everted rims (Basden et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the specimen and citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The scan of ANU V3628 reveals delicate endochondral bone laminae filling the eyestalk attachment area.
claims.source: The scan of ANU V3628 reveals delicate endochondral bone laminae filling the eyestalk attachment area (Figure 3A, eys), forming a rough surface as seen on other articular surfaces in many osteichthyans.
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the CT scan data.

claims.claim: The pituitary vein is continuous between the orbits in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: The pituitary vein is continuous between the orbits, and is connected to the hypophysial chamber by a median hypophysial vein (Figure 5D, hyp.v).
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the CT scan data.

claims.claim: The pituitary vein is connected to the hypophysial chamber by a median hypophysial vein in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: The pituitary vein is continuous between the orbits, and is connected to the hypophysial chamber by a median hypophysial vein (Figure 5D, hyp.v).
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the CT scan data.

claims.claim: The condition of the pituitary vein in 'Ligulalepis' is similar to the transverse pituitary vein in placoderms.
claims.source: This condition is similar to the transverse pituitary vein in placoderms, for example Brindabellaspis (Young, 1980), Parabuchanosteus (Young, 1979), Jagorina (Stensiö, 1969) and probably Romundina (Dupret et al., 2017; Goujet and Young, 2004).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison with placoderm anatomy.

claims.claim: The condition of the pituitary vein in 'Ligulalepis' contrasts with other crown gnathostomes in which the pituitary vein enters the hypophysial chamber directly.
claims.source: The condition in 'Ligulalepis' contrasts with other crown gnathostomes in which the pituitary vein enters the hypophysial chamber directly (e.g. Maisey, 2005; Maisey, 2007; Holland, 2014; Giles and Friedman, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison with other gnathostome anatomy.

claims.claim: The trochlear (IV) nerve enters the orbit dorsal to the eyestalk attachment area in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: The trochlear (IV) nerve enters the orbit dorsal to the eyestalk attachment area, some way posterior to the dorsal myodome (my.IV) and anterior cerebral vein (Figures 3 and 4C,D).
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the CT scan data.

claims.claim: The revised position of the trochlear (IV) nerve in 'Ligulalepis' reflects the general gnathostome condition.
claims.source: This revised position of the trochlear (IV) nerve (i.e. posterodorsal to the eyestalk) reflects the general gnathostome condition (Chang, 1982; Gardiner, 1984; Maisey, 2005; Young, 1979), but the position of the myodome anterior to the orbit is more similar to that of osteichthyans.
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison with other gnathostome anatomy.

claims.claim: The large foramen in the orbit most likely transmitted the mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: As such, the large foramen in the orbit most likely transmitted the mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve (Figures 4C–E and 5A,C, Vmd).
claims.evidence: This is based on reinterpretation of the anatomy.

claims.claim: The morphology of the mandibular nerve canal in 'Ligulalepis' is similar to that seen in chondrichthyans.
claims.source: This morphology is similar to that seen in chondrichthyans (e.g. Cladodoides: Maisey, 2005; 'Cobelodus': Maisey, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison with chondrichthyan anatomy.

claims.claim: Posterior to the root of the trigeminal nerve, a canal (r.lat) leaves the anterior face of the utricular region and enters the 'trigemino-facialis chamber' in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: Posterior to the root of the trigeminal nerve, a canal (r.lat) leaves the anterior face of the utricular region and enters the "trigemino-facialis chamber" (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the CT scan data.

claims.claim: The canal r.lat is interpreted as the root of the anterior lateral line nerves in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: This is interpreted as the root of the anterior lateral line nerves, in a similar position as in other early osteichthyans (Jarvik, 1980; Chang, 1982; Giles and Friedman, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is based on interpretation of the anatomy and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: An additional canal (mcv) exits the cranial cavity from the midpoint of the cerebellum and enters the 'trigemino-facialis chamber' at a steep angle in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: An additional canal (mcv) exits the cranial cavity from the midpoint of the cerebellum and enters the "trigemino-facialis chamber" at a steep angle (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the CT scan data.

claims.claim: The canal mcv is interpreted as the middle cerebral vein in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: Due to its position and orientation, this is interpretated as the middle cerebral vein.
claims.evidence: This is based on interpretation of the anatomy.

claims.claim: The canal ventral to the hyomandibular facet can be confirmed as the hyomandibular trunk of the facial nerve (VIIhm) in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: The canal ventral to the hyomandibular facet intersects the ventral portion of the jugular canal and can be traced to the ventral otic fissure. It can be confirmed as the hyomandibular trunk of the facial nerve (VIIhm; Basden and Young, 2001: figs. 2,3).
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the CT scan data and confirmation of previous identification.

claims.claim: The foramen identified by Basden and Young (2001) as for the glossopharyngeal nerve is in fact the posterior exit of the jugular canal in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: The foramen identified by Basden and Young ([2001]: figs 2,3) as for the glossopharyngeal nerve is in fact the posterior exit of the jugular canal (Figure 4B,F, jug.c); the glossopharyngeal nerve presumably exited through the otic-occipital fissure.
claims.evidence: This is based on reinterpretation of the anatomy.

claims.claim: The internal carotids enter the braincase through two foramina flanking the median hypophysial opening in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: As outlined by Basden and Young (2001), the internal carotids enter the braincase through two foramina flanking the median hypophysial opening before giving off the efferent pseudobranchial and ophthalmic artery (Figure 4B, epsb, Figure 4C, opha).
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the CT scan data and confirmation of previous description.

claims.claim: There is no evidence of a parabasal canal carrying the palatine artery anterior to the internal carotid entry point in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: As in chondrichthyans (Maisey, 2005; Maisey, 2007), but unlike in osteichthyans (Chang, 1982; Gardiner, 1984) and placoderms (Hu et al., 2017; Young, 1980), there is no evidence of a parabasal canal carrying the palatine artery anterior to this point.
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the CT scan data and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: The overall endocast of 'Ligulalepis' is short and broad, particularly the otic region.
claims.source: Overall, the endocast of 'Ligulalepis' is short and broad, particularly the otic region (Figure 7A,B).
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the cranial endocast.

claims.claim: The proportions of the endocast of 'Ligulalepis' are similar to early chondrichthyans.
claims.source: The proportions occupied by different regions are similar to early chondrichthyans, with the forebrain section comprising less than 20% of the total length, the midbrain section around 15%, and the hindbrain section some 65%.
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison with chondrichthyan endocasts.

claims.claim: A distinct depression in the roof of the cranial cavity, medial to the otic capsule, is in fact the crus commune of the anterior and posterior semicircular canal in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: A distinct depression in the roof of the cranial cavity, medial to the otic capsule, was considered by (Zhu et al. ([2010], fig. 4c) to be evidence of a lateral cranial canal. This embayment is in fact the crus commune of the anterior and posterior semicircular canal (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is based on reinterpretation of the anatomy.

claims.claim: The region of the forebrain in 'Ligulalepis' is relatively wide.
claims.source: This region in 'Ligulalepis' is relatively wide (Figure 7A,B), comparable to the forebrain in placoderms such as Macropetalichthys (Stensiö, 1963a) and chondrichthyans such as Orthacanthus (Schaeffer, 1981).
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the endocast and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: The short olfactory tracts of 'Ligulalepis' are similar to those of placoderms and chondrichthyans.
claims.source: The short olfactory tracts are similar to those of placoderms, for example Buchanosteus (Young, 1979) and Kujdanowiaspis (Stensiö, 1963a), as well as chondrichthyans such as Cladodoides (Maisey, 2005) and Orthacanthus (Schaeffer, 1981), but also some sarcopterygians such as Tungsenia (Lu et al., 2012a2012) and Qingmenodus (Lu et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: A small canal for the terminal nerve (0) exits from the anterior face of the forebrain, between the olfactory tracts, in AM-F101607.
claims.source: A small canal for the terminal nerve (0) exits from the anterior face of the forebrain, between the olfactory tracts, in AM-F101607.
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the CT scan data.

claims.claim: The telencephalon is the widest and highest portion of the forebrain in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: The telencephalon is the widest and highest portion of the forebrain. At its widest point it measures 6 mm in AM-F101607.
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the endocast.

claims.claim: The telencephalon is developed into slight lobes dorsolaterally in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: It is developed into slight lobes dorsolaterally; these may represent olfactory bulbs (Figure 7A, olf.b).
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the endocast.

claims.claim: The hypophysis is oriented ventrally in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: The hypophysis is oriented ventrally, in agreement with the generalised osteichthyan condition (e.g. Youngolepis: Chang, 1982; Mimipiscis: Giles and Friedman, 2014), but unlike the posterodorsally-oriented hypophysis seen in Cladodoides (Maisey, 2005).
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the endocast and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: The midbrain cavity is not differentiated into separate recesses for each optic lobe in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: The midbrain cavity is not differentiated into separate recesses for each optic lobe (Figure 7A, opt.l), which appears to be the general gnathostome condition.
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the endocast and comparison with other gnathostomes.

claims.claim: The oculomotor nerve does not bifurcate along its course in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: More ventrally, the oculomotor (III) nerve leaves the midbrain and enters the orbit (Figure 5A,C); there is no evidence that this nerve bifurcated along its course.
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the CT scan data.

claims.claim: The hindbrain is the widest portion of the endocast in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: The hindbrain is the widest portion of the endocast and would have housed the metencephalic and myelencephalic brain regions in life.
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the endocast.

claims.claim: The cerebellum extends anterior to the labyrinth in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: The cerebellum extends anterior to the labyrinth (Figure 7A,B, cer), as in chondrichthyans (e.g. Cladodoides, Maisey, 2005) and, to a lesser extent, sarcopterygians (e.g. Eusthenopteron, Jarvik 1980).
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the endocast and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: The profundus nerve leaves the cranial cavity separately from the trigeminal nerve in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: The profundus nerve (prof) leaves the cranial cavity separately from the trigeminal nerve (V) and enters the orbit (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the CT scan data.

claims.claim: The separation of the trigeminal and profundus nerves is the plesiomorphic state for crown gnathostomes.
claims.source: The cranial nerve configuration seen in 'Ligulalepis' adds to a growing body of evidence from fossil endocranial studies that the separation of the trigeminal and profundus nerves is indeed the plesiomorphic state for crown gnathostomes (Chang, 1982; Giles and Friedman, 2014; Maisey, 2005).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison with other fossil taxa and inference about character polarity.

claims.claim: The posterior dorsal fontanelle is trapezoidal in outline in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: The posterior dorsal fontanelle is trapezoidal in outline (Figure 7A, pdf).
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the endocast.

claims.claim: ANU V3628 appears to have a lateral cranial canal.
claims.source: ANU V3628 appears to have a lateral cranial canal (Figure 7B,D, lcc?), as in actinopterygians (Giles et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the CT scan data.

claims.claim: In ANU V3628, the dorsal part of the groove for the posterior cerebral vein contains a large foramen in the same position to the opening for the lateral cranial canal in Moythomasia and Mimipiscis.
claims.source: In ANU V3628, the dorsal part of this groove contains a large foramen, most clearly developed on the left side (Figure 8C,D), in the same position to the opening for the lateral cranial canal in Moythomasia (Gardiner, 1984, fig. 27) and Mimipiscis (Gardiner, 1984, fig. 11).
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the CT scan data and comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: The lateral cranial canal may have been variable in its development in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: The lateral cranial canal may have been variable in its development, as has been suggested for Mimipiscis (Gardiner, 1984).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison between the two specimens and citation to similar variability in another taxon.

claims.claim: The labyrinth region in 'Ligulalepis' is well preserved in AM-F101607.
claims.source: The labyrinth region in 'Ligulalepis' is well preserved in AM-F101607 (Figure 7A,C), with three complete, slender semicircular canals present, and all carrying small expansions for ampullae.
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the CT scan data.

claims.claim: The anterior semicircular canal is anteroposteriorly long, but does not extend far ventrally in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: The anterior semicircular canal (asc) is anteroposteriorly long, but does not extend far ventrally.
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the endocast.

claims.claim: The posterior semicircular canal is tall dorsoventrally, but anteroposteriorly very short in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: In contrast, the posterior semicircular canal (psc) is tall dorsoventrally, but anteroposteriorly very short.
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the endocast.

claims.claim: The ventral position of the posterior canal in 'Ligulalepis' is reminiscent of that in placoderms, chondrichthyans, early sarcopterygians and the early actinopterygian Mimipiscis.
claims.source: This ventral position of the posterior canal is reminiscent of that in placoderms (e.g. Dicksonosteus; Goujet, 1984), chondrichthyans (Schaeffer, 1981; Maisey, 2007), early sarcopterygians (e.g. Youngolepis; Chang, 1982) and, to a slightly lesser extent, in the early actinopterygian Mimipiscis (Giles and Friedman, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: The external canal is positioned obliquely at an angle of about 30 degrees from the cranial cavity in 'Ligulalepis'.
claims.source: Strikingly, the external canal is positioned obliquely at an angle of about 30 degrees from the cranial cavity, and completes nearly a full circle before re-entering the vestibule (Figure 7A,C).
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the endocast.

claims.claim: The general morphology of the labyrinth in 'Ligulalepis' recalls that of an early chondrichthyan such as Cladodoides or perhaps even Acanthodes.
claims.source: The general morphology of the labyrinth, including the dorsoventrally extensive posterior canal, which projects above the endocranial roof as well as below the cerebellar floor, and the inclined external canal, recalls that of an early chondrichthyan such as Cladodoides (Maisey, 2005) or perhaps even Acanthodes (Davis et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: The labyrinth of 'Ligulalepis' is far removed from that seen in Mimipiscis, or sarcopterygians such as Eusthenopteron and Devonian lungfishes.
claims.source: The labyrinth is far removed from that seen in Mimipiscis (Giles and Friedman, 2014), or sarcopterygians such as Eusthenopteron and Devonian lungfishes (Clement and Ahlberg, 2014; Clement et al., 2016; Jarvik, 1980).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison with other taxa.

claims.claim: The parsimony analysis retrieves Dialipina, 'Ligulalepis', and 'psarolepids' as successively branching sister taxa to the osteichthyan crown node.
claims.source: The parsimony analysis retrieves Dialipina, 'Ligulalepis', and 'psarolepids' as successively branching sister taxa to the osteichthyan crown node (Figure 10A).
claims.evidence: This is the result of the parsimony phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: Support for the clade that comprises crown osteichthyans is low in the parsimony analysis, with Bremer support of 1 and a bootstrap of just 4.
claims.source: However, support for the clade that comprises crown osteichthyans (as retrieved from this analysis) is low, with Bremer support of 1 and a bootstrap of just 4.
claims.evidence: This is based on the support values calculated from the parsimony analysis.

claims.claim: A stem actinopterygian position for 'Ligulalepis' requires a single additional step in the parsimony analysis.
claims.source: A stem actinopterygian position for 'Ligulalepis' requires a single additional step, and the grouping of 'Ligulalepis' and actinopterygians was found in 18% of the bootstrap replicates.
claims.evidence: This is based on constrained phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: A single additional step is required to place 'psarolepids' on the sarcopterygian stem in the parsimony analysis.
claims.source: A single additional step is required to place 'psarolepids' on the sarcopterygian stem, and this grouping is found in 16% of bootstrap replicates.
claims.evidence: This is based on constrained phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: The Bayesian analysis retrieves 'psarolepids' on the sarcopterygian stem with moderately strong support (pp = 0.94).
claims.source: The Bayesian analysis retrieves 'psarolepids' on the sarcopterygian stem with moderately strong support (pp = 0.94, Figure 11).
claims.evidence: This is the result of the Bayesian phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: 'Ligulalepis' is resolved as a stem osteichthyan in the 50% majority rule tree from the Bayesian analysis.
claims.source: 'Ligulalepis' is resolved as a stem osteichthyan in the 50% majority rule tree (Figure 11), although the crown osteichthyan clade has weak support (0.61).
claims.evidence: This is the result of the Bayesian phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: An actinopterygian position for 'Ligulalepis' has a posterior probability of 0.22 in the Bayesian analysis.
claims.source: However, an actinopterygian position for 'Ligulalepis' has a posterior probability of 0.22.
claims.evidence: This is based on the posterior probabilities from the Bayesian analysis.

claims.claim: 'Ligulalepis' is recovered as a stem osteichthyan in the phylogenetic analysis, specifically as the sister lineage to 'psarolepids' plus crown Osteichthyes.
claims.source: 'Ligulalepis' is recovered as a stem osteichthyan in the phylogenetic analysis, specifically as the sister lineage to 'psarolepids' (Guiyu, Sparalepis, Psarolepis, Achoania) plus crown Osteichthyes (Figures 9 and 10).
claims.evidence: This is the main result of the phylogenetic analyses.

claims.claim: Cranial features previously suggested as linking 'Ligulalepis' with actinopterygians are now better considered to be general osteichthyan characters or of uncertain polarity.
claims.source: Cranial features previously suggested as linking 'Ligulalepis' with actinopterygians (Basden and Young, 2001) are now better considered to be general osteichthyan characters (e.g. dermal ornament) or of uncertain polarity (skull roof pattern and overall structure).
claims.evidence: This is based on reinterpretation of the anatomical features in light of new data and phylogenetic context.

claims.claim: Of the three characters proposed by Lu et al., 2017 as uniting ray-finned fishes inclusive of Meemannia, 'Ligulalepis' lacks two: posteriorly expanded tabulars and a spiracular canal.
claims.source: Of the three characters proposed by Lu et al., 2017 as uniting ray-finned fishes inclusive of Meemannia, 'Ligulalepis' lacks two: posteriorly expanded tabulars (supratemporals of actinopterygians) and a spiracular canal.
claims.evidence: This is based on observation of the specimens and comparison with the character list.

claims.claim: The development of a lateral cranial canal can be expressed simply in terms of the degree of ossification of the dorsal otic region.
claims.source: Gardiner (1984) suggested that the lateral cranial canal can be expressed simply in terms of the degree of ossification of the dorsal otic region.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Gardiner, 1984.

claims.claim: The two specimens of 'Ligulalepis' seem to confirm the idea that the lateral cranial canal can be expressed in terms of the degree of ossification.
claims.source: The two specimens of 'Ligulalepis' seem to confirm this idea, with the development of a lateral cranial canal variable between specimens, and the extent of the canal and perichondral lining also variable within a specimen.
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of the two specimens.

claims.claim: An actinopterygian identification for 'Ligulalepis' is at odds with the lack of pore canal network.
claims.source: Moreover, an actinopterygian identification for 'Ligulalepis' is also at odds with the lack of pore canal network.
claims.evidence: This is based on the absence of a feature typically found in actinopterygians.

claims.claim: Constraining 'Ligulalepis' to the actinopterygian stem also leads to 'psarolepids' branching from the sarcopterygian stem.
claims.source: Topology tests reveal that the relationships of these early osteichthyans are somewhat interdependent, as constraining 'Ligulalepis' to the actinopterygian stem also leads to 'psarolepids' branching from the sarcopterygian stem, necessitating independant origins of a number of characters in 'psarolepids' and non-osteichthyan gnathostomes (cf. Lu et al., 2017), and of tooth enamel in actinopterygians and sarcopterygians.
claims.evidence: This is based on the results of constrained phylogenetic analyses.

claims.claim: Characters that support a stem osteichthyan position for 'Ligulalepis' are also found in Psarolepis and Achoania.
claims.source: This is because characters that support a stem osteichthyan position for 'Ligulalepis' (i.e. the presence of an eyestalk and short olfactory tracts) are also found in Psarolepis and Achoania (Zhu et al., 2001; Zhu et al., 2013) and only support a stem osteichthyan position if all these taxa are recovered on the stem.
claims.evidence: This is based on character distribution and phylogenetic reasoning.

claims.claim: Evidence for a stem osteichthyan position for 'psarolepids' is now accumulating.
claims.source: Evidence for a stem osteichthyan position for 'psarolepids' is now accumulating, with characters such as dorsal fin spines, a median dorsal plate and absence of tooth enamel supporting this relationship (Qu et al., 2015; Zhu et al., 2009; Lu et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claims.claim: The current phylogenetic hypothesis is that 'Ligulalepis' is a stem osteichthyan.
claims.source: In summary, our current phylogenetic hypothesis is that 'Ligulalepis' is a stem osteichthyan.
claims.evidence: This is the conclusion of the phylogenetic analyses.

claims.claim: While an actinopterygian affinity for 'Ligulalepis' requires only one extra step, this position seems to be at odds with the distribution of anatomical features amongst early osteichthyans.
claims.source: While an actinopterygian affinity requires only one extra step, this position seems to be at odds with the distribution of anatomical features amongst early osteichthyans.
claims.evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic analysis and anatomical comparisons.

claims.claim: The skulls investigated are not necessarily disqualified from belonging to the same animal as the scales described for Ligulalepis.
claims.source: The skulls investigated herein are not necessarily disqualified from belonging to the same animal as the scales described for Ligulalepis (Schultze, 1968).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the possibility of association.

claims.claim: Disassociated material cannot be unequivocally attributed to the same taxon.
claims.source: However, we follow Giles et al., 2015c in maintaining the position that disassociated material cannot be unequivocally attributed to the same taxon.
claims.evidence: This is a methodological principle supported by citation.

claims.claim: The presence of superimposed layers of enamel applied directly to each other is known only in actinopterygians.
claims.source: While 'ganoine' encompasses multiple character states, some of which are general for osteichthyans (e.g. the presence of enamel, multiple layers of enamel) the presence of superimposed layers of enamel applied directly to each other is known only in actinopterygians.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the distribution of a histological character.

claims.claim: Ligulalepis—the scale-based taxon—is an actinopterygian.
claims.source: This indicates that Ligulalepis—that is the scale-based taxon—is an actinopterygian, at odds with the osteichthyan identification of 'Ligulalepis'—that is the cranium-based taxon.
claims.evidence: This is based on the histological features of the scales.

claims.claim: A scale-based Ligulalepis is problematic, as constituent species are erected on the basis of widespread (and often plesiomorphic characters) and span from the Ludlow of China to the Emsian of Australia.
claims.source: A scale-based Ligulalepis is still problematic, however, as constituent species are erected on the basis of widespread (and often plesiomorphic characters) and span from the Ludlow of China (Wang and Dong, 1989) to the Emsian of Australia (Schultze, 1968).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the taxonomic problems with the scale-based taxon.

claims.claim: Acrodin is a highly mineralized capping tissue restricted to actinopterygians crownward of Cheirolepis.
claims.source: Acrodin is a highly mineralized capping tissue restricted to actinopterygians crownward of Cheirolepis (Friedman and Brazeau, 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Friedman and Brazeau, 2010.

claims.claim: The tooth and jaw fragment attributed to Ligulalepis most likely does not belong to the same taxon as the skulls investigated.
claims.source: It is unclear which characters were used to identify this specimen as Ligulalepis, but it most likely does not belong to the same taxon as the skulls investigated herein.
claims.evidence: This is based on the presence of acrodin in the tooth, which is not consistent with a stem osteichthyan position.

claims.claim: Both specimens of 'Ligulalepis' came from the limestone outcrops on private land at the southern end of Goodradigbee Inlet, Wee Jasper, New South Wales, Australia.
claims.source: Both specimens came from the limestone outcrops on private land (Cathles' 'Cooradigbee' property) at the southern end of Goodradigbee Inlet, Wee Jasper, New South Wales, Australia.
claims.evidence: This is information about the provenance of the specimens.

claims.claim: ANU V3628 was found in the Bloomfield Limestone Member of the Taemas Formation near Rocky Flat.
claims.source: ANU V3628 was found in the Bloomfield Limestone Member of the Taemas Formation near Rocky Flat, and AM-F101607 was probably from a similar horizon, possibly at Caravan Point about 300 m to the north, although precise locality and horizon were not recorded for this specimen (although most likely from the Emsian pireneae-serotinus condont zone).
claims.evidence: This is information about the stratigraphic provenance of the specimens.

claims.claim: AM-F101607 was scanned at the Australian National University High Resolution Micro X-ray Computed Tomography facility with a resultant scan resolution of 30.4 microns.
claims.source: AM-F101607 was scanned at the Australian National University (ANU) High Resolution Micro X-ray Computed Tomography facility (Sakellariou et al., 2004) with a resultant scan resolution of 30.4 microns (SI:1).
claims.evidence: This is information about the methods used to scan the specimen.

claims.claim: ANUV3628 was scanned at Adelaide Microscopy on a Skyscan 1076 with a resultant voxel size of 8.5 microns.
claims.source: ANUV3628 (SI:2) was scanned at Adelaide Microscopy on a Skyscan 1076. Specimen to source distance was 121 mm, camera to source distance was 161 mm. Source voltage was 100kV, and current 100 µA. 393 projections were taken on a Hamamatsu Orca-HRF camera. The resultant voxel size was 8.5 microns.
claims.evidence: This is information about the methods used to scan the specimen.

results.result: CT scanning of two 'Ligulalepis' specimens (AM-F101607 and ANU V3628) reveals novel skull roof anatomy including suture patterns, a pineal foramen, and the previously unknown anterior portion of the skull roof.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C38 describe direct observations from CT scan data of both specimens, documenting skull roof sutures, the pineal foramen, and the anterior skull roof region. These anatomical observations are well-supported by the imaging data presented in Figures 1-2.

results.result: The snout of 'Ligulalepis' has a sharply downturned anterior face with distinctive ornamentation changes, and the nostril configuration shows the excurrent nostrils lying within the orbits with the posterior nostril opening directly into the orbit without an endoskeletal postnasal wall.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C45 describe anatomical features of the snout and nostril configuration based on direct observation of the specimens and CT scan data. The comparison with other taxa (C41, C45) provides phylogenetic context. These observations are well-documented in Figure 3.

results.result: The sensory canal system of 'Ligulalepis' shows distinctive features including a two-section supraorbital canal, unbranched tubuli of varying sizes, anterior opening of supraorbital canals to the dorsal surface, absence of a preopercular canal, and presence of a 'P' canal in ANU V3628.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C55 describe the sensory canal anatomy based on CT scan observations and comparisons with other taxa. The observations are directly supported by the imaging data shown in Figures 1 and 3, with appropriate comparative context from the literature.

results.result: The braincase of 'Ligulalepis' is well ossified and comprises the basisphenoid, orbitotemporal, and otic regions, with the orbital region being large (nearly half of total braincase length), the ethmoid region short, and the posterior/ventral portions absent.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C60 and C71 describe the overall braincase structure based on direct observation of both specimens. These are straightforward anatomical descriptions supported by the CT scan data and illustrated in Figures 4-7.

results.result: The ethmoid region of 'Ligulalepis' shows a complex arrangement of nerves and foramina, including a canal for the anterior cerebral vein (present only on the left side), an internal course for the superficial ophthalmic nerve, and multiple foramina in the nasal capsule for branches of the profundus, maxillary, and buccal nerves.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C70 describe the ethmoid region anatomy based on CT scan data and reinterpretation of previous identifications. The observations are supported by detailed segmentation shown in Figures 4-6, though some identifications involve inference about nerve pathways (C62, C65, C66, C68, C69).

results.result: The orbitotemporal region of 'Ligulalepis' exhibits a distinctive vascular and neural anatomy including an eyestalk attachment area with endochondral bone, a placoderm-like transverse pituitary vein connected to the hypophysial chamber by a median hypophysial vein, and a chondrichthyan-like arrangement of cranial nerves and blood vessels.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C89 describe the orbitotemporal anatomy based on CT scan observations and comparisons with placoderms, chondrichthyans, and osteichthyans. The observations are well-documented in Figures 3-6, with appropriate comparative context. Some identifications involve reinterpretation of previous work (C80, C87).

results.result: The cranial endocast of 'Ligulalepis' is short and broad with proportions similar to early chondrichthyans, featuring a relatively wide forebrain with short olfactory tracts, a ventrally oriented hypophysis, undifferentiated optic lobes, and separate profundus and trigeminal nerves.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C105 describe the cranial endocast anatomy based on CT scan data and comparisons with other taxa. The observations are well-supported by Figure 7 and detailed segmentations in Figures 4-6. Claim C104 makes a broader inference about character polarity that is supported by comparative evidence.

results.result: The lateral cranial canal shows variable development between the two 'Ligulalepis' specimens, with ANU V3628 showing clearer evidence of the structure than AM-F101607, supporting the hypothesis that this feature's development relates to the degree of ossification.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C106-C108, C126-C127 describe the variable presence of the lateral cranial canal based on comparison of the two specimens. The observations are supported by CT scan data shown in Figures 7-8, with appropriate citation to similar variability in other taxa (C108, C126).

results.result: The labyrinth system of 'Ligulalepis' shows a chondrichthyan-like morphology with an anteroposteriorly long anterior semicircular canal, a dorsoventrally tall posterior semicircular canal in a ventral position, and an obliquely positioned external canal at about 30 degrees, differing markedly from actinopterygians and sarcopterygians.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C115 describe the labyrinth anatomy based on CT scan observations and extensive comparisons with other taxa. The observations are well-documented in Figure 7 and supported by appropriate comparative context from the literature.

results.result: Parsimony phylogenetic analysis places 'Ligulalepis' as a stem osteichthyan, specifically as the sister taxon to 'psarolepids' plus crown osteichthyans, though support for the crown osteichthyan clade is low (Bremer support of 1, bootstrap of 4) and a stem actinopterygian position requires only one additional step.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8, C116-C119, C123 describe the results of the parsimony phylogenetic analysis. The results are clearly presented in Figure 10 with appropriate support values. The weak support is acknowledged (C117), and alternative placements are tested (C118-C119).

results.result: Bayesian phylogenetic analysis retrieves 'psarolepids' on the sarcopterygian stem with moderately strong support (pp = 0.94), while 'Ligulalepis' is resolved as a stem osteichthyan in the 50% majority rule tree with weak support (pp = 0.61), and an actinopterygian position has a posterior probability of 0.22.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C120-C122 describe the results of the Bayesian phylogenetic analysis. The results are clearly presented in Figure 11 with appropriate posterior probability values. The difference between parsimony and Bayesian results regarding 'psarolepids' is noted (C9).

results.result: Features previously suggested as linking 'Ligulalepis' with actinopterygians are reinterpreted as general osteichthyan characters or of uncertain polarity, and the distribution of anatomical features (including eyestalk presence and short olfactory tracts) supports a stem osteichthyan position, though an actinopterygian affinity requires only one extra step.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C133 present the phylogenetic interpretation of the anatomical data. The reinterpretation is based on the new anatomical observations and phylogenetic analyses. The reasoning is logical and supported by character distribution patterns and topology tests, though the weak phylogenetic support is acknowledged.

results.result: The scale-based taxon Ligulalepis is identified as an actinopterygian based on the presence of superimposed layers of enamel, while the cranium-based 'Ligulalepis' is a stem osteichthyan, and a tooth/jaw fragment with acrodin likely does not belong to the same taxon as the skulls, indicating that disassociated material cannot be unequivocally attributed to the same taxon.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C140 address the taxonomic implications of disassociated material. The reasoning is based on histological features (C136-C137, C139) and methodological principles (C135). The conclusion that the scale-based and cranium-based taxa are different is logically supported, though it creates taxonomic complexity (C138).

results.result: The skull of 'Ligulalepis' (AM-F101607) has significantly expanded knowledge of early osteichthyan anatomy, but its phylogenetic position has remained uncertain.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2 are introductory statements supported by the detailed anatomical descriptions in the manuscript and the history of conflicting phylogenetic placements discussed in the introduction (C15-C32).

results.result: Background on osteichthyan diversity and early fossil record: 98% of living vertebrate species belong to Osteichthyes, the earliest osteichthyans are late Silurian (~425 Ma), and the early actinopterygian fossil record is poorly understood with the oldest putative actinopterygian being Meemannia (~415 Ma).
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C14 provide background information supported by citations to the literature. These are well-established facts about vertebrate diversity and the fossil record.

results.result: Historical review of phylogenetic placements of early osteichthyans (Dialipina, Psarolepis, Guiyu) and 'Ligulalepis', showing conflicting interpretations ranging from stem actinopterygian to stem sarcopterygian to stem osteichthyan across different studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C32 provide a comprehensive review of the phylogenetic history of early osteichthyans and 'Ligulalepis', all supported by appropriate citations to the literature. This establishes the context for the current study.

results.result: Both specimens of 'Ligulalepis' came from the Bloomfield Limestone Member of the Taemas Formation at Wee Jasper, New South Wales, Australia, and were scanned using micro-CT with resolutions of 30.4 microns (AM-F101607) and 8.5 microns (ANU V3628).
results.evaluation: Claims C141-C144 provide methodological information about specimen provenance and scanning parameters. These are straightforward factual statements about the materials and methods used in the study.
